# IS-IS Basics

## Learning goals

- Place IS-IS next to OSPF as a second link-state IGP: LSPs, flooding, SPF, but a different addressing and level model.
- Read a NET (area + system ID + NSEL) and choose level-1, level-2 or level-1-2 on purpose.
- Write a minimal FRR `isisd` configuration for a point-to-point triangle, including wide metrics and IPv4/IPv6.
- Know the operational traps: mismatched levels, narrow versus wide metrics, the overload bit, and hello authentication that drops adjacencies.

Version note: FRR and Containerlab/netlab were **not installed** on the writing host, and no IS-IS adjacency was formed (no root, no installs). Commands, defaults and configuration syntax are taken from FRR’s current `isisd` documentation, ISO 10589, RFC 1195 and RFC 5308, and from netlab’s IS-IS module listing. Run the lab on your Containerlab or netlab host and treat the “expected” show output as a checklist, not as a capture from this machine.

[OSPF Basics](01-ospf-basics.qmd) already covers link-state versus distance-vector, areas, cost and a triangle lab. This chapter does not repeat that pedagogy; it maps the same ideas onto IS-IS.

## Why another link-state IGP?

IS-IS (Intermediate System to Intermediate System) is specified in ISO 10589. RFC 1195 added IPv4 (“integrated IS-IS”); RFC 5308 describes IPv6. Like OSPF, each router floods a link-state database and runs SPF. Unlike OSPF:

- Packets are not encapsulated in IP. IS-IS PDUs are exchanged directly over the link (on Ethernet, as an 802.3 / 802.2 LLC frame to the AllIS and AllL1/AllL2 multicast addresses). A broken IP stack can still form an IS-IS adjacency. A capture filter is `isis` or `clns`, not `ip proto 89`.
- Addressing of the protocol itself is ISO: each router has a **NET**, not an OSPF router-id plus area.
- The two-level hierarchy is **level-1** (inside an area) and **level-2** (the backbone). A router is L1, L2, or L1/L2. There is no named “area 0” that every ABR must touch in the OSPF sense; the backbone is the set of L2 adjacencies.
- Information is carried in **TLVs**, which is why IPv6, TE, SR and SRv6 were added without changing the core FSM.

ISPs and large fabrics often prefer IS-IS for that extensibility and for the fact that IPv4 and IPv6 can share one SPF (or use multi-topology, RFC 5120, when you do *not* want them to). The protocol is not Cisco-only and is first-class in FRR.

## The NET

A Network Entity Title is an NSAP that identifies this IS. The usual lab form is 8–20 bytes, written in dotted hex, and ends with NSEL `00`:

```text
49.0001.1921.6800.1001.00
│  │    │              └─ n-selector (00 = the router itself)
│  │    └──────────────── system ID (6 bytes) — must be unique in the domain
│  └───────────────────── area (here 0001; can be longer)
└──────────────────────── AFI 49 = private (ISO)

```

Pick a convention and keep it. Two common lab habits:

- Encode an IPv4 loopback in the system ID: `10.0.0.1` → `0100.0000.0001`.
- Use simple integers: `r1` → `0000.0000.0001`.

FRR takes the whole NET under `router isis`:

```
router isis lab
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
```

FRR does not support multiple IS-IS *processes* yet, but you still have to name the instance (`lab` above). That name must match `ip router isis lab` / `ipv6 router isis lab` on the interfaces. A VRF-aware instance is `router isis lab vrf RED`.

## Levels, DIS and circuit type

| Role | Adjacencies | Typical use |
|------|-------------|-------------|
| `level-1` | L1 only, same area | Stub or access area |
| `level-2-only` | L2 only | Backbone / inter-area |
| `level-1-2` (default-ish behaviour on many platforms) | Both | Area border, leaks L1 prefixes into L2 when configured |

On broadcast media IS-IS elects a **DIS** (Designated Intermediate System) per level, by priority then system ID. The DIS does not become a permanent transit stub the way an OSPF DR can; it mainly originates the pseudonode LSP and paces CSNPs. On point-to-point links, skip the DIS: in FRR, `isis network point-to-point`. That is the right type for almost every veth or Containerlab link.

Hello, CSNP and PSNP timers, and the hello multiplier, are per interface and per level. FRR defaults to the three-way handshake on P2P (RFC 5303) and to periodic CSNPs even on P2P; you can turn the latter off to save bandwidth once you know why they exist (a periodic CSNP is how a neighbor notices a hole in its LSP database).

## Metrics: use wide

ISO 10589 metrics were 6-bit (**narrow**, max 63). RFC 5305 wide metrics are 24-bit. FRR’s default `metric-style` is **wide**. Do not mix narrow and wide in a lab unless you are practising a migration (`metric-style transition` sends and accepts both).

With wide metrics, the value `16777215` (`2^24 - 1`) is still advertised but **ignored in SPF**, as RFC 5305 requires. That is how you take a link out of the topology without tearing the adjacency. FRR’s `advertise-high-metrics` (RFC 3277) sets 63, 62 or 16777215 depending on style, to shift traffic off a node you are draining.

The **overload bit** (`set-overload-bit`) tells others not to use this IS as transit. `set-overload-bit on-startup (0-86400)` holds the bit after boot so BGP or LDP can settle first. Use it; do not just slash all interface metrics and hope.

## A triangle in FRR (not run)

Three point-to-point links, one area, level-2 only, IPv4 and IPv6 on each router. This is the documentation form of the lab; deploy it with Containerlab + FRR or with netlab’s `module: [ isis ]`.

```
! r1 — /etc/frr/frr.conf  (integrated config; zebra must be up first)
interface eth1
 ip router isis lab
 ipv6 router isis lab
 isis network point-to-point
 isis circuit-type level-2-only
 isis metric 10
!
interface eth2
 ip router isis lab
 ipv6 router isis lab
 isis network point-to-point
 isis circuit-type level-2-only
 isis metric 10
!
interface lo
 ip router isis lab
 ipv6 router isis lab
 isis passive
!
router isis lab
 net 49.0001.0000.0000.0001.00
 is-type level-2-only
 metric-style wide
 hostname dynamic
 log-adjacency-changes
```

`r2` and `r3` differ only in the NET system ID (`…0002.00`, `…0003.00`) and in which interfaces face whom. Enable `isisd` in `/etc/frr/daemons` alongside `zebra`.

On a running router you would check, in order:

```bash
vtysh -c 'show isis neighbor'
vtysh -c 'show isis interface detail'
vtysh -c 'show isis database'
vtysh -c 'show isis topology'
vtysh -c 'show isis route'
```

Expect: two neighbors in `Up` (or `Full`-equivalent adjacency state in the neighbor listing), a database with an LSP per IS, a topology that lists both peers, and routes to the other loopbacks. If a neighbor is missing, check NET uniqueness, matching levels, point-to-point vs broadcast, and whether both `ip router isis` and addresses are present.

### The same graph in netlab (not run)

```yaml
defaults.device: frr
provider: clab
module: [ isis ]
isis:
  net: 49.0001.0000.0000.0000.00
  type: level-2

nodes:
  r1:
  r2:
  r3:

links:
  - r1-r2
  - r2-r3
  - r3-r1
```

Confirm attribute names with `netlab show modules -m isis` on your version before you rely on `isis.type` / `isis.net`. netlab will allocate system IDs and render the FRR snippets. Add a `validate:` plugin or an `exec:` ping once the module lab comes up.

## IPv4, IPv6 and one SPF

`ip router isis lab` carries IPv4; `ipv6 router isis lab` carries IPv6. On an interface with both, a single adjacency can advertise both families. Multi-topology (`topology ipv6-unicast` in FRR) *splits* the SPF so an IPv6-only link does not black-hole IPv4.

FRR also has `isis ipv4-over-ipv6-nexthop`: IPv4 routes via the neighbor’s IPv6 link-local when the link has no IPv4 address (Linux 5.2+). Enable it on **every** router on that link, or one side will forward IPv4 into a neighbor that will not. This is the IS-IS analogue of BGP RFC 8950, and it has the same operational rule: both ends, or neither.

## Fast reroute, SR and the rest (awareness)

FRR IS-IS implements local LFA, remote LFA (LDP), TI-LFA, a TE database, SR-MPLS (experimental, RFC 8667) and SRv6 (RFC 9352). Those are later studies; the [Segment Routing, SRv6, and TI-LFA](06-segment-routing-srv6-ti-lfa.qmd) chapter already covers the ideas. Get a clean L2 triangle and `show isis route` before you turn `segment-routing on`.

Authentication (clear text, HMAC-MD5, or RFC 5310 key chains) and RFC 7602 extended sequence numbers are how you stop a lab from accepting replayed hellos. Enable `send` on everyone before `verify` on anyone — the same “both ends” rule.

## Common mistakes

- Two routers with the same system ID. The database looks haunted; neighbors flap or LSPs overwrite each other.
- `is-type level-1` on one side and `level-2-only` on the other. No adjacency, no error you will notice unless you read `show isis neighbor` and the hello log.
- Leaving the default broadcast type on a veth, then debugging DIS election that the lab did not need.
- Narrow metrics in a topology that also has wide-metric routers.
- Forgetting `isis passive` on the loopback, so IS-IS hellos go out a stub interface — or the opposite, forgetting it and never advertising the loopback.
- Starting `isisd` before `zebra`, or restarting zebra and not isisd.
- Setting the overload bit for a maintenance window and never clearing it.

## Boring rule

One unique NET per IS, matching levels on the link, point-to-point on lab veths, wide metrics, and a `show isis neighbor` / `show isis database` / `show isis route` pass before you talk about policy or SR. If the LSP database does not agree, SPF will not save you.

## Try this

1. Deploy the triangle with netlab or Containerlab. Capture `show isis neighbor` and `show isis database`. Shut one link and watch SPF and the remaining path.
2. Change r3 to `is-type level-1` only, leave r1 and r2 at level-2, and predict which adjacencies die.
3. Set `isis metric 100` on one side of a link and not the other. IS-IS is not required to have symmetric costs; look at each router’s `show isis route`.
4. Set `set-overload-bit` on r2 and confirm r1–r3 no longer transit r2, while r2 can still reach others.
5. Enable IPv6 on all three, then an IPv6-only link, with and without multi-topology, and see whether IPv4 is dragged into a black hole.
